triage.name: Osteoarthritis
triage.reason: Very common joint disease with classic mechanical pain, activity limitation and exam findings; excellent musculoskeletal interview and exam case.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Prevalence rises steadily with age and is very common after age 60
Before age 50 it affects men and women about equally; after age 50 it is more common in women
More common in people with physically demanding jobs or a history of joint injury

risk_factors.text: Prior joint injury or surgery (meniscus tear, ACL tear, fracture)
Repetitive overuse of a joint from work or sports

family_history: Osteoarthritis in a parent or sibling, especially hand or knee osteoarthritis
social_history: Occupations with repetitive kneeling, squatting, lifting or climbing
Participation in high-impact or pivoting sports

chief_complaints.text: My knee hurts when I walk
My joints are stiff in the morning
It's hard to get up from a chair or go up stairs
My hands ache and look knobby
My hip is sore and it's hard to put on my shoes

hpi.onset: Gradual, over months to years, often without a single remembered injury
hpi.duration: Chronic, usually present for months to years by the time of diagnosis
hpi.progression: Slowly worsens over time; pain becomes more frequent with activity and may eventually occur at rest or at night
hpi.location: Most often knees, hips, hands (especially the base of the thumb and the joints closest to the fingertips), neck and lower back; usually one or a few joints rather than many at once
hpi.radiation: Usually none; hip pain may be felt in the groin, buttock or thigh
hpi.quality: Aching, dull, deep soreness; sometimes sharp with certain movements
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate early on, increasing to moderate or severe with advanced disease; often described as 3–6/10 at rest and worse with use
hpi.timing: Worse with activity and toward the end of the day; brief morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes; may have pain at night with severe disease
aggravating: Walking or standing for a while
Getting up from a low chair
Gripping or pinching with the hands
relieving: Gentle movement after the joint loosens up

associated_symptoms.text: Joint stiffness after resting that eases within about 30 minutes
Swelling of the joint after heavy use
Grinding, cracking or popping in the joint with movement
Feeling that the joint may give way or is unstable
Decreased range of motion, such as trouble bending the knee fully

pertinent_negatives: Joint redness, warmth or marked swelling suggesting infection or crystal arthritis
Fever, chills or feeling systemically unwell
Prolonged morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Pain and swelling in many joints on both sides at once
Severe pain that wakes the patient from sleep early in the disease
Recent tick bite, rash or travel to an area with tick-borne illness
Recent joint injection, surgery or penetrating injury
Back pain with bowel or bladder changes or saddle numbness

positives.text: Crepitus or grinding in the joint

negatives: Severe pain at rest early in the disease
Muscle weakness or numbness in the limb
argues_against: Symmetrical small-joint arthritis of recent onset

negatives: Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
argues_against: Nerve compression or spinal cord problem

atypical.how_it_differs: Pain may be less clearly related to activity, and the patient may report mainly stiffness, unsteadiness or falls rather than joint pain.
Symptoms tend to be more severe and start earlier, especially in the knees, and weight loss often improves pain.
Osteoarthritis is rare in children; when it occurs it is usually secondary to a prior injury, deformity or a genetic joint condition, and the child may limp or avoid using the limb.

general.mild: Comfortable, well-appearing, no distress; normal gait or only slight favoring of the affected joint
general.moderate: Mild discomfort with movement, may limp or use the railing on stairs; not systemically ill
general.severe: Visible limp or need for a cane, grimaces when rising or bearing weight, but no fever or toxicity
general.critical: Not applicable; osteoarthritis is not a critical illness. If the patient appears toxic, febrile or acutely unable to bear weight, consider septic arthritis or another cause.

findings.maneuver: Palpate along the joint line of the affected joint (e.g., the medial and lateral knee joint lines)
findings.finding: Focal tenderness along the joint line

findings.maneuver: Place a hand on the joint and move it through its range of motion
Measure active and passive range of motion of the affected joint
findings.finding: Reduced range of motion, often with a firm endpoint

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the joint margins
findings.finding: Bony enlargement or prominence at the joint margins (osteophytes)

findings.maneuver: Perform a bulge or ballottement test on the knee, or palpate for fluctuance
findings.finding: Small joint effusion, usually without marked warmth or erythema

findings.maneuver: Inspect the alignment of the lower extremities while the patient stands
Inspect and palpate the distal interphalangeal joints of the hands
findings.finding: Bony nodules at the distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden nodes)

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the proximal interphalangeal joints of the hands
findings.finding: Bony nodules at the proximal interphalangeal joints (Bouchard nodes)

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the base of the thumb (first carpometacarpal joint)
findings.finding: Bony prominence and tenderness at the base of the thumb

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking and rising from a chair
findings.finding: Antalgic gait or difficulty rising, favoring the affected joint

findings.maneuver: Palpate the affected joint for warmth and compare with the opposite side
findings.finding: No marked warmth or erythema over the joint

findings.maneuver: Assess general appearance, temperature and vital signs
findings.finding: No fever, chills or systemic toxicity

findings.maneuver: Examine the small joints of both hands and feet for symmetrical swelling
findings.finding: No symmetrical soft-tissue swelling of the MCP joints or wrists

findings.maneuver: Test sensation, strength and reflexes in the affected limb
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss or reflex change

labs.caveat: Usually normal or only mildly elevated. A markedly elevated CRP suggests an inflammatory or infectious arthritis rather than osteoarthritis.
Normal or only mildly elevated in osteoarthritis; a high ESR points toward an inflammatory arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica or infection.
Ordered when gout is a consideration. Normal or near-normal in osteoarthritis; a normal level during an acute attack does not fully exclude gout.
A normal white count is expected in osteoarthritis. Leukocytosis with fever should prompt evaluation for septic arthritis.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or before medications that are unsafe in pregnancy.

imaging.study: Weight-bearing x-ray of the affected joint (knee, hip, or hand)

findings.text: Joint space narrowing, often asymmetric and worse in the weight-bearing compartment
Osteophytes (bone spurs) at the joint margins
Subchondral sclerosis (increased bone density just beneath the cartilage)
Varus or valgus malalignment of the knee on standing films

imaging.preferred_when: When another cause is suspected (meniscal tear, ligament injury, avascular necrosis, tumor, or infection)

findings.text: Meniscal or ligamentous tear if a mechanical injury is also present

imaging.preferred_when: Guidance for joint aspiration or injection; assessing effusion and synovitis

findings.text: Osteophytes visible at the joint margin

imaging.preferred_when: Preoperative planning or when complex bony anatomy must be defined

initial.test: Weight-bearing x-ray of the affected joint (knee, hip, or hand)
initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis and grades structural severity; weight-bearing views are needed to assess joint space.
Helps exclude an inflammatory or infectious arthritis when the presentation is atypical.
initial.only_if: the joint is warm, swollen or the presentation suggests inflammation

initial.why: Supports exclusion of inflammatory arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica or infection.
initial.only_if: the joint is warm, swollen or the presentation suggests inflammation

initial.why: Evaluates for gout when the joint is acutely painful, red or swollen.
Rules out pregnancy before imaging or medications that are unsafe in pregnancy.

supporting.why: Clarifies alternative or coexisting pathology when symptoms are disproportionate to x-ray findings or a mechanical injury is suspected.
supporting.only_if: another cause is suspected or the diagnosis remains unclear

supporting.why: Can confirm an effusion and guide aspiration or injection.
supporting.only_if: an effusion is present or a joint injection is planned

supporting.why: Looks for leukocytosis if infection is a concern.

not_indicated.why: Not needed for the diagnosis; obtain only for medication monitoring or preoperative assessment.
Rarely adds information beyond x-ray except for surgical planning.

decision_points: A hot, red, swollen joint with fever requires urgent aspiration to exclude septic arthritis before assuming osteoarthritis.
Weight-bearing x-rays are preferred over non-weight-bearing films for assessing knee joint space.
Prolonged morning stiffness over an hour, symmetric small-joint swelling or systemic symptoms should prompt testing for inflammatory arthritis.
Pregnancy test before imaging or medications that are unsafe in pregnancy.

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of osteoarthritis
criteria.summary: Diagnosis is clinical, based on activity-related joint pain, brief morning stiffness, reduced function and characteristic exam findings, supported by typical x-ray changes. No single blood test confirms it.
items: Joint pain worse with activity and relieved by rest
Morning stiffness lasting less than about 30 minutes
Crepitus, bony enlargement, reduced range of motion or joint-line tenderness on exam
X-ray showing joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis or cysts
Absence of systemic inflammation or features of inflammatory arthritis

differential.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
differential.why_considered: Joint pain and swelling in an adult, especially in the hands
differential.trigger: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour with symmetric small-joint swelling

history: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Pain and swelling in many joints on both sides at once
Fatigue, low-grade fevers, unintentional weight loss
Improves with activity rather than worsening with use
exam: Symmetrical soft-tissue swelling of the MCP joints and wrists
Warm, boggy joints rather than hard bony enlargement
Rheumatoid nodules
Ulnar deviation or swan-neck deformities in advanced disease
imaging: Symmetric joint space narrowing with marginal erosions

differential.name: Septic arthritis
differential.why_considered: Acute joint pain and swelling, especially in a single joint
differential.trigger: Hot, red, swollen joint with fever or inability to bear weight

history: Abrupt onset over hours to days
Fever, chills, feeling systemically unwell
Recent joint injection, surgery, penetrating injury or bacteremia
Immunosuppression, diabetes, or prosthetic joint
exam: Marked warmth, erythema and tense effusion
Severe pain with any passive movement
Refusal to bear weight
Fever and systemic toxicity
labs: Synovial fluid with white count over 50,000/mm3, mostly neutrophils, and positive Gram stain or culture
imaging: X-ray usually normal early; may show effusion
Ultrasound showing effusion and guiding aspiration
MRI showing marrow edema and effusion if diagnosis is unclear

differential.name: Gout
differential.why_considered: Acute painful, swollen joint, often in the lower extremity

history: Sudden severe attacks reaching peak intensity within hours
Classically first MTP joint, but any joint possible
Attacks triggered by alcohol, purine-rich meals, diuretics or dehydration
Painful attacks separated by completely symptom-free periods
exam: Exquisitely tender, red, hot, swollen joint during an attack
Tophi on the ear, fingers or elbows in chronic disease
No bony enlargement or crepitus between attacks
labs: Elevated uric acid between attacks (may be normal during an attack)
Synovial fluid with needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals
imaging: Normal joint space until late disease

differential.name: Psoriatic arthritis
differential.why_considered: Joint pain and swelling in a patient with skin or nail changes

history: Personal or family history of psoriasis
Joint pain and swelling, sometimes asymmetric or in the fingers and toes
Morning stiffness and fatigue
Back or heel pain suggesting enthesitis
exam: Psoriatic plaques on elbows, knees, scalp or gluteal cleft
Nail pitting, onycholysis or oil spots
Dactylitis (sausage digit)
Enthesitis at the Achilles or plantar fascia
labs: Elevated ESR and CRP during flares
Uric acid may be mildly elevated
imaging: Erosions with adjacent new bone formation (pencil-in-cup)

differential.name: Polymyalgia rheumatica
differential.why_considered: Pain and stiffness in an older adult, especially in the shoulders and hips

history: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness
Stiffness worst in the morning and after inactivity, lasting more than an hour
Age over 50, often over 60
Constitutional symptoms such as fatigue, low-grade fever and weight loss
exam: Pain with active range of motion but preserved passive range
No true joint swelling or bony enlargement
Possible temporal artery tenderness if giant cell arteritis coexists
imaging: No erosive or degenerative joint changes
Ultrasound or MRI may show bursitis or tenosynovitis

history: Widespread pain in many areas for more than three months
Fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive fog
Pain not clearly related to activity or a single joint
Symptoms often fluctuate with stress and weather
exam: Diffuse tenderness without joint swelling, warmth or effusion
Normal joint range of motion
No crepitus or bony enlargement
imaging: Normal joint x-rays without joint space narrowing or osteophytes

differential.name: Avascular necrosis of the hip
differential.why_considered: Hip or groin pain in an adult, especially with risk factors

history: Deep groin or buttock pain that may be present at rest
Risk factors: corticosteroid use, alcohol use, sickle cell disease, prior trauma
Pain may progress rapidly over weeks to months
exam: Pain with internal rotation and abduction of the hip
Antalgic gait
Limited range of motion, especially internal rotation
imaging: X-ray may be normal early; later shows sclerosis, subchondral crescent sign and collapse
MRI is the most sensitive test, showing marrow edema and the double-line sign

differential.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
differential.why_considered: Back and leg pain in an older adult, often with activity limitation

history: Leg pain, numbness or heaviness brought on by walking and relieved by sitting or leaning forward
Symptoms better when bending forward or pushing a shopping cart
Back pain with neurogenic claudication
exam: Often normal strength and reflexes at rest
Symptoms reproduced with lumbar extension
Wide-based gait or positive Romberg in severe cases
imaging: MRI showing central canal, lateral recess or foraminal narrowing
X-ray may show degenerative changes but does not show the canal

severity.mild: Intermittent joint pain with activity, brief morning stiffness under 30 minutes, minimal functional limitation, and x-rays showing mild joint space narrowing or small osteophytes.
severity.moderate: Frequent pain with activity and some pain at rest, reduced range of motion, crepitus and bony enlargement, difficulty with stairs or rising from a chair, and x-rays showing moderate joint space narrowing with osteophytes and sclerosis.
severity.severe: Persistent pain at rest and at night, marked functional limitation or need for a cane or walker, visible deformity or malalignment, large effusions, and x-rays showing marked joint space narrowing with bone-on-bone contact.
severity.critical: Not applicable; osteoarthritis is not a life-threatening condition. A patient who appears toxic, febrile or acutely unable to bear weight should be evaluated for septic arthritis or another cause.

red_flags.finding: Hot, red, swollen joint with fever or chills
red_flags.meaning: Suggests septic arthritis or crystal arthritis; requires urgent joint aspiration.

red_flags.finding: Acute inability to bear weight after trauma
red_flags.meaning: Suggests fracture or ligamentous injury; needs imaging.

red_flags.finding: Night pain that wakes the patient from sleep, especially with weight loss or night sweats
red_flags.meaning: Suggests infection, malignancy or another systemic process.

red_flags.finding: Prolonged morning stiffness lasting more than an hour with symmetric small-joint swelling
red_flags.meaning: Suggests inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

red_flags.finding: Back pain with bowel or bladder changes, saddle numbness or progressive weakness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests cauda equina syndrome; requires emergency evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Rapidly progressive joint destruction or deformity over weeks
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an inflammatory or neuropathic process rather than typical osteoarthritis.

complications.name: Chronic pain and reduced quality of life
Functional decline and disability
clues: Difficulty walking, climbing stairs or rising from a chair
Need for a cane or walker

complications.name: Secondary bursitis or tendonitis
clues: Localized swelling and tenderness near the joint

special_populations.differences: Pain may be less clearly activity-related; patients may present with stiffness, unsteadiness or falls rather than joint pain. Comorbidities and polypharmacy complicate treatment, and the risk of falls and fractures is higher.
Symptoms tend to be more severe and start earlier, especially in the knees. Weight loss of even 5–10% can meaningfully improve pain and function.

Osteoarthritis is rare in children; when it occurs it is usually secondary to prior injury, deformity or a genetic joint condition. The child may limp or avoid using the limb, and other causes of childhood arthritis should be excluded.
Joint laxity and weight gain can worsen symptoms, especially in the knees and hips. Imaging and medication choices must account for fetal safety; acetaminophen is preferred for pain.
Diabetes and metabolic syndrome are associated with more severe and more rapidly progressive osteoarthritis. Neuropathy may mask or alter pain perception.

key_questions.question: Which joint or joints are bothering you, and is it one side or both?
key_questions.looking_for: One or a few joints, often knees, hips, hands, neck or low back; not many small joints symmetrically

key_questions.question: Does the pain get worse when you use the joint and better when you rest?
key_questions.looking_for: Mechanical pattern: worse with activity, relieved by rest

key_questions.question: How long does the stiffness last after you get up in the morning or after sitting?
key_questions.looking_for: Brief stiffness, less than about 30 minutes; over an hour suggests inflammatory arthritis

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over months to years with slow progression

key_questions.question: What activities are hard for you now, like stairs, getting out of a chair, or gripping things?
key_questions.looking_for: Functional limitation in weight-bearing or gripping tasks

key_questions.question: Do you hear or feel grinding, cracking or popping in the joint?
Does the joint ever swell after you use it a lot, or feel like it might give way?
Have you ever injured or had surgery on this joint?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior meniscal tear, ACL tear, fracture or joint surgery

key_questions.question: Has your weight changed, or has a doctor talked with you about your weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Obesity or excess weight, especially with knee or hip symptoms

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have arthritis or joint problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of osteoarthritis, especially hand or knee

key_questions.question: What do you do for work, and do you do a lot of kneeling, squatting, lifting or climbing?
key_questions.looking_for: Repetitive joint overuse from work or sports

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or a joint that is hot, red and suddenly very swollen?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; if present, consider septic arthritis or crystal arthritis and aspirate urgently

key_questions.question: Does the pain wake you from sleep, or have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; night pain with weight loss suggests infection or malignancy

key_questions.question: Any back pain with numbness in the groin area, or trouble controlling your bowel or bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; if present, evaluate urgently for cauda equina syndrome

reasoning_points: Mechanical joint pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest
Brief morning stiffness lasting less than about 30 minutes
Gradual onset over months to years in a middle-aged or older adult
Involvement of one or a few weight-bearing or commonly used joints such as knees, hips or hands
Exam findings of joint-line tenderness, crepitus, reduced range of motion or bony enlargement
Absence of fever, systemic illness, or a symmetric inflammatory small-joint pattern
Weight-bearing x-ray showing joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis or cysts
Normal or only mildly elevated inflammatory markers when checked

easy: Older adult with chronic knee pain worse with walking and stairs
Crepitus and bony enlargement on exam
Weight-bearing x-ray showing joint space narrowing and osteophytes
medium: Hand osteoarthritis with Heberden and Bouchard nodes and thumb base pain
Hip osteoarthritis presenting with groin or buttock pain rather than knee pain
Obesity with early-onset knee symptoms and functional limitation
Mildly elevated ESR or CRP that raises concern for inflammatory arthritis
hard: Older adult with stiffness and unsteadiness rather than clear activity-related pain
Normal x-ray early in the disease despite typical symptoms
Coexisting gout or rheumatoid arthritis confusing the picture
Back or leg pain from lumbar spinal stenosis mistaken for hip osteoarthritis
Younger adult with post-traumatic osteoarthritis after a prior joint injury
